rows.evidence: Q1: Sections III-IV, Tables I-VII, Figs 5-11 - the authors built three data loggers with low-cost resistive sensors, ran two gravimetric calibration experiments in clay soil and a 19 April-3 May 2016 evaluation in three soil pots, comparing sensor readings against weight-based moisture and computing percent error.
rows.notes: The study reports only sensor accuracy and precision (calibration curves, percent error averaging 13.7-30% across three devices, sources of error: corrosion, ion concentration, temperature, installation). It does not measure irrigation water use, water efficiency or water savings, nor does it test the sensors in an irrigation-control or developing-region farmer context; the remarks about low cost and developing countries are introduction statements, not findings. It concludes the sensors are unsuitable for continuous or high-accuracy irrigation control, which cuts against the claim. Sensor accuracy is at most a precondition of the claimed water-efficiency effect, so upstream is set to true.

notes: Full text appears complete (conference paper, 5 pages). Study is a laboratory/greenhouse sensor evaluation with no irrigation performance or water-use outcome.
